items.titel: Protesters to join nationwide march as France braces for day of strike action
items.anriss: Hospital workers, air traffic and rail staff expected to join strikes amid renewed protests over education and rising living costs

absaetze.t: Hundreds of thousands are expected to march in demonstrations across France as trade unions call for a nationwide strike expected to extend to hospital workers, air traffic control, the post office, teachers and rail staff.

President Emmanuel Macron’s final months in office continue to be marred by domestic crises, as high school students protesting over poor teaching conditions have been joined by workers in weekly protests over the cost of living. Meanwhile, the government is struggling to pass a belt-tightening budget in a divided parliament as public debt approaches 120% of economic output.

Ahead of Thursday’s strike action, France’s four main rail unions said that the government’s proposed budget cuts would “worsen poverty, slash social security, freeze state workers’ salaries and dry up investment needed for environmental measures”.

Amid the renewed protests centred on living costs, public spending cuts and the troubled education system, the far-right, anti-immigration candidate Marine Le Pen is polling high for the 2027 presidential election to replace Macron next spring.

High school students continued to blockade schools over overcrowded classes and dilapidated buildings, saying the government’s proposed measures on capping some class sizes and loaning funds to regional authorities to fix schools were not enough. University students joined in blockading some faculties. Trade unions from across the political landscape joined in a call for strikes over the rising cost of living, with private schools’ teachers unions also joining strikes alongside state school teachers.
Rights’ groups protested over what they said was heavy policing and an “authoritarian” attempt by Macron’s executive to clamp down on the right to demonstrate.

The French Human Rights League said there was an “authoritarian shift” to stifle “any dissenting voice” as the government put in place heavy policing and authorities issued restrictions on demonstrating in city centres, as well as curfews in certain areas.

Sophie Binet, the head of the leftwing CGT union, said: “We’re living at a very serious time with a very dangerous authoritarian drift from the government”, criticising decisions by authorities in cities such as Rennes, Toulouse and Lyon to push demonstrations out of city centres.
Marylise Léon, the head of the moderate CFDT trade union, said: “The principle of a demonstration is its visibility.”

The national rail operator SNCF said there would be “disturbances” to train services on regional lines and some parts of the greater Paris area. Dockers said there would be disruption in French ports. The education ministry said it expected almost 18% of nursery and primary school teachers to strike. Trade unions said they also expected secondary teachers to take part in Thursday’s strike.

items.titel: Après les midterms, une fenêtre pour la relation transatlantique ?
items.anriss: Le résultat historique des élections de mi-mandat américaines ouvre une période complètement nouvelle pour la suite du second mandat de Donald Trump.

absaetze.t: Testez le Grand Continent. Les idées et les analyses qu’on ne trouve nulle part. Mais que vous verrez bientôt partout. Dans votre boîte mail à partir de 8 euros par mois
Le résultat historique des élections de mi-mandat américaines ouvre une période complètement nouvelle pour la suite du second mandat de Donald Trump.
Sur le plan domestique, le président américain se trouve désormais très affaibli par une défaite qui sonne avant tout comme un référendum contre sa personne, ses pratiques et son bilan.

Les conséquences de l’élection sont durables : les nouveaux sénateurs sont élus pour six ans et siégeront jusqu’à la fin de la présidence de Donald Trump, mais aussi pendant tout le mandat présidentiel suivant.
Les résultats des midterms sont aussi très importants pour l’Europe.

Sur le plan institutionnel d’abord, les démocrates disposent désormais au Congrès des moyens de contrôler beaucoup plus étroitement l’action de Donald Trump, même si l’exécutif américain est moins encadré par la Constitution en matière extérieure et militaire que sur les sujets domestiques.

Ensuite, plus fondamentalement et à long terme, l’élection est la démonstration de la résilience et de la vitalité de la démocratie américaine (déjà illustrée par le rôle des contre-pouvoirs depuis deux ans), à de très nombreux égards : la forte participation, la façon dont les élections se sont tenues sans violence ni perturbation, l’acceptation des résultats par le Président, la diversité et la nouveauté des profils des candidats élus (pas seulement pour le Congrès, mais aussi aux fonctions de gouverneurs, par exemple), l’incapacité des sommes considérables d’argent privé dépensées dans la campagne par des milliardaires comme Elon Musk ou Vivek Ramaswamy à peser sur les résultats.

Enfin, cette nouvelle donne au Congrès offre des opportunités inédites à l’Europe, pour autant que celle-ci fasse des propositions novatrices, quitte à revisiter certaines de ses propres références, et change d’échelle pour répondre à l’ampleur des enjeux.
Des garanties institutionnelles à construire

Sur l’avenir de la relation transatlantique, c’est d’abord aux Américains, et à la nouvelle majorité au Congrès, qu’il revient de rétablir la confiance. Les Européens, comme tous les partenaires traditionnels des États-Unis, peuvent à juste titre douter de l’intérêt de resserrer les liens avec un pays qui a confié deux fois à Donald Trump les fonctions suprêmes.
Certes, au regard de leur ampleur, les résultats pourraient laisser augurer la défaite de ses héritiers à la présidentielle, dans deux ans.

Mais il ne peut être exclu que l’un d’eux, inspiré par ses méthodes et sa pratique du pouvoir, accède un jour à la Maison-Blanche. Les fractures américaines qui expliquent l’émergence politique de Donald Trump se sont développées sur plus d’une génération. Les réduire prendra plus d’un mandat présidentiel, comme l’a montré la présidence de Joe Biden.

Le contexte nouveau issu des midterms, mais aussi les réflexions menées aux États-Unis sur le nécessaire renforcement des institutions pour prévenir l’autoritarisme, permettent cependant l’émergence de solutions et de garanties nouvelles pour les Européens et les partenaires des États-Unis.

Prenons la politique commerciale, domaine dans lequel Donald Trump a fait plier l’Europe avec un accord très déséquilibré, sans précédent pour l’Union européenne : la Constitution en confie la compétence au Congrès.

Donald Trump a pu agir en s’appuyant sur des délégations de compétences en matière de droits de douane, conférées par des textes souvent anciens, pour certains sortis de l’oubli par Robert Lighthizer, son représentant au commerce lors de son premier mandat. Si la Cour suprême s’est récemment opposée au président américain sur la façon dont il mettait en œuvre ces délégations, elle n’a pas condamné leur usage en tant que tel. Lors de son premier mandat, le président avait déjà fait beaucoup de mal aux intérêts européens, en particulier français, en les activant, sans en outrepasser le cadre.

Il devient aujourd’hui possible de traiter ces risques de façon structurelle pour l’avenir. Le Congrès peut modifier ces délégations pour contraindre l’exécutif à obtenir son accord avant d’instituer des mesures commerciales contre les alliés des États-Unis. Il existe d’ailleurs déjà un précédent. Avant de devenir secrétaire d’État, lorsqu’il était sénateur de Floride, Marco Rubio avait fait adopter une disposition interdisant au président américain de quitter l’OTAN sans l’approbation préalable du Congrès.

Le Congrès va par ailleurs engager un travail institutionnel pour renforcer l’encadrement des pouvoirs de l’exécutif et prévenir les risques autoritaires à l’avenir. Un tel processus s’était brièvement engagé en 2021, après l’attaque contre le Capitole. Il reprendra sur un large champ : le droit de grâce du président, y compris envers lui-même, l’étendue et les limites de son autorité sur les agences fédérales indépendantes, l’obligation pour l’exécutif de mettre en œuvre les décisions budgétaires votées par le Congrès, son pouvoir de nomination, autant de domaines dans lesquels Donald Trump a cherché à s’affranchir des normes de la démocratie américaine.

Dans un tel contexte, des propositions visant à encadrer l’exécutif pour garantir la prévisibilité, la qualité et la stabilité des relations avec les alliés des États-Unis trouveront un écho favorable au Congrès.
Ce que les démocrates reprochent à l’Europe
Si les premiers pas pour rétablir la confiance doivent venir des Américains, les Européens, pour leur part, ne doivent pas méconnaître la dégradation sensible de l’image qu’ont d’eux les démocrates.

De nombreux responsables démocrates influents estiment en effet que l’Union s’est montrée beaucoup moins exigeante et critique envers Donald Trump qu’à l’égard de Joe Biden. Ils soulignent que lors de l’adoption du plus grand plan de lutte contre le changement climatique jamais voté aux États-Unis (l’Inflation Reduction Act), les pays européens, qui dénonçaient jusque-là l’inaction américaine, ont surtout réagi négativement, critiquant des dispositions unilatérales et protectionnistes, avant de se montrer bien plus discrets sur la politique climatique de Donald Trump.

Ils avancent aussi que l’Union a refusé de s’engager avec Joe Biden dans des rapprochements en matière de politique industrielle, au motif que les propositions américaines n’étaient pas conformes au droit du commerce international, pour conclure ensuite à Turnberry avec Donald Trump un accord bilatéral très déséquilibré, pourtant ouvertement contraire aux principes de l’OMC.

Au Congrès, et à la Maison-Blanche s’ils la reconquièrent dans deux ans, les démocrates placeront aussi la relation avec la Chine au centre de leur agenda avec l’Union, comme question stratégique essentielle, voire comme préalable au reste du dialogue.

Sur ce point aussi, la déception à l’égard de l’Europe est profonde. Les démocrates n’ont pas compris pourquoi, pendant le mandat de Joe Biden, l’Union s’est tenue à distance de l’agenda politique et commercial américain à l’égard de la Chine.

Tout en reconnaissant la responsabilité centrale des États-Unis dans la lourde erreur de jugement qui voulait que l’intégration de la Chine dans les échanges internationaux amène celle-ci à devenir plus démocratique à l’intérieur et moins nationaliste à l’extérieur, ils estiment que l’Union a refusé de partager ce diagnostic pour des raisons idéologiques, liées à son attachement à la libéralisation des échanges.

Un dossier juridique en particulier, très peu connu en Europe, a beaucoup pesé dans cette prise de distance, d’autant qu’une grande partie des élites démocrates sont des juristes de formation : le soutien apporté par la Commission européenne, au nom de la défense du multilatéralisme, aux décisions de l’organe d’appel du système de règlement des différends de l’OMC, y compris lorsque celui-ci a refusé de considérer, dans un contentieux sur les subventions octroyées par la Chine, les compagnies publiques chinoises comme des organismes publics, au motif qu’elles n’exerçaient pas d’autorité gouvernementale, une interprétation qui ne figure pas dans les textes de l’OMC.
Chine, climat : les terrains d’une coopération nouvelle
Le durcissement en cours de l’Union face aux pratiques économiques, commerciales et monétaires de la Chine semble aujourd’hui ouvrir la voie à de nouvelles coopérations.

Avec plus de dix ans de retard sur les États-Unis, les pays européens jusqu’ici les moins résolus à l’égard du mercantilisme chinois, comme l’Allemagne, semblent désormais estimer à leur tour que le niveau atteint par les subventions, les surcapacités de production, les stratégies de vente à perte des entreprises chinoises menacent directement la pérennité des industries et des activités économiques en Europe, le tissu social et productif et, in fine, la stabilité politique des démocraties.

Par ailleurs, l’acceptation sociale et politique de la transition énergétique, déjà complexe et difficile, serait vouée à l’échec, en Europe comme en Amérique, si la lutte contre le changement climatique se traduisait au final par la domination de monopoles chinois, la disparition de secteurs économiques entiers, la dépendance à l’égard d’entreprises chinoises capables d’interrompre leurs livraisons à des fins de pression politique.

Pour leur part, les démocrates vont chercher à reprendre leur stratégie de réindustrialisation au bénéfice des régions les moins favorisées, autour de vastes investissements en matière environnementale et climatique, pour améliorer les conditions de vie des classes populaires américaines, et répondre aux fragilités sociales et politiques qui ont nourri l’essor politique de Donald Trump.
C’est donc notamment sur ces questions que pourrait se concentrer, dès à présent, la reprise de la coopération transatlantique.

En matière climatique, les États-Unis et l’Union européenne n’avaient pas pu se mettre d’accord, à la fin du mandat de Joe Biden, sur un traitement commun des importations selon leur contenu en carbone, dans certains secteurs comme l’acier et l’aluminium. L’Union pourrait proposer de reprendre ces discussions.

Plus largement, l’Union a institué un mécanisme d’ajustement carbone à la frontière. Aux États-Unis, des projets de loi déposés au Congrès, y compris avec le soutien de sénateurs républicains, portent la même vision ; bloqués par l’administration Trump, ils pourraient désormais avancer. Un travail fondateur de rapprochement pourrait être engagé.

De façon plus ambitieuse encore, les États-Unis et l’Union européenne pourraient travailler conjointement à un projet d’union douanière, couvrant les produits les plus importants pour la transition énergétique (les véhicules électriques, les panneaux solaires, les batteries, etc.). Dans ces secteurs, les États-Unis et l’Europe mettraient en œuvre de façon coordonnée (en associant d’autres États qui souhaiteraient se joindre à eux) les mêmes instruments (droits antidumping, mesures antisubventions), à l’égard des pays tiers qui subventionnent massivement leurs productions nationales.

Les Américains ont un intérêt essentiel à ce que l’économie européenne ne disparaisse pas sous la pression chinoise ; les Européens, eux, ont intérêt à ancrer leur résolution nouvelle à l’égard de la Chine dans des accords contractuels avec d’autres pays comme les États-Unis, car il n’est pas sûr qu’ils trouvent en eux-mêmes la fermeté suffisante pour faire face aux menaces chinoises. Cette union douanière permettrait de retrouver un levier de pression systémique à la hauteur des enjeux.
Lever les obstacles, des deux côtés de l’Atlantique

Les obstacles à un rapprochement transatlantique n’en restent pas moins considérables. Donald Trump reste au pouvoir pour deux ans. Il existe désormais un profond passif. Les incertitudes sont nombreuses des deux côtés de l’Atlantique.

items.titel: Canada spat exposes widening rift between Merz and von der Leyen

absaetze.t: A dispute over what to call the EU’s future relationship with Canada is deepening a split between European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, four diplomats told POLITICO.

Berlin and Brussels are at loggerheads over von der Leyen’s proposal to make Canada an “associate member” of the EU, with tensions worsening after the Commission president touted the phrase at a summit in Montreal — just hours after a German-led push removed the wording from a joint statement approved by 27 EU capitals.

Merz previously floated “associate member” as a status for Ukraine, as it works toward fully joining the bloc. After the idea was roundly rejected, including by Kyiv itself, officials in Berlin see von der Leyen’s push to use the term for Canada as a rebuke of the German chancellor’s initiative.
The clash over the phrasing is illustrative of a growing divide between Merz and von der Leyen toward how the bloc should be governed.

Berlin has said it won’t approve the EU’s next long-term budget, proposed by the Commission at around €2 trillion, unless “hundreds of billions” are shaved off the total amount. And von der Leyen’s proposal for a European Security Council has failed to gain traction in Germany, where the government has embraced a separate format with France and the U.K. for sensitive Ukraine-related matters.

“There is this institutional dilemma between Brussels and Berlin,” said Jan Techau, head of Germany for the Eurasia group and a former speechwriter for the German defense ministry. “Von der Leyen has taken a strongly integrationist approach to the EU while Merz has completely developed away from this and talks about the nation states as the primary driver of EU policy.”
A representative for Merz did not respond to POLITICO’s request for comment.
What’s in a name?
Neither Berlin nor Brussels are giving ground on the “associate member” issue.

Berlin reiterated its opposition at a meeting of EU ambassadors on Wednesday, two of the diplomats told POLITICO. But the Commission president has no intention of abandoning the label, a person familiar with her thinking said. They were granted anonymity, like others in this article, to describe the sensitive diplomacy.

“We’re really focusing on building on the foundations that were set last week at the summit,” said Paula Pinho, chief spokesperson for the Commission, adding that Berlin and Brussels share the same basic goals regarding EU-Canada ties.
A German diplomat said: “There is no difference in substance. We both committed to form a unique partnership that we don’t have with any other country outside the European Union.”
The difference comes down to fine print, as von der Leyen’s definition of the associate member term — as applied to Canada — precludes the status from being offered to Ukraine, two EU diplomats said.

Instead of an intermediate step on the way into the EU, complete with prizes such as observer status in the European Council, associate member status would be granted to a country that could never be fully admitted to the EU — as von der Leyen acknowledged in her Montreal speech.
Von der Leyen’s use of the term thwarted Berlin’s logic. “Germany had different plans for associate membership — and still does,” said one of the diplomats.

Techau said Berlin and Brussels share “ideological overlap on many issues,” including party affiliation — both Merz and von der Leyen belong to Germany’s conservative Christian Democratic Union Party. “They often have similar views and even on ideas like this,” he said, referring to warmer ties with Ottawa.

Yet the Canada issue has played out in “an exemplary way,” he said. While von der Leyen sees this as “a big geopolitical gain for her and the Commission,” Merz has “proven disappointing to people in Brussels who hoped he would take a more integrationist approach to the EU, and this has been driven entirely by domestic prerogatives.”

For Techau, the label dispute is a proxy for the wider argument running through core debates such as the budget and the bloc’s security: whether the EU should be driven more by its common institutions or by its national governments.
“The issue is, in many ways, ‘unresolvable,’” Techau said.
Zoya Sheftalovich and Seb Starcevic contributed reporting from Brussels.

items.titel: Serbia detains police officers over alleged use of force against protesters
items.anriss: Interior ministry claims suspects tortured and intimidated protesters detained in garage of government compound

absaetze.t: Serbian authorities detained nine active police officers and one former officer on Wednesday for ⁠allegedly using excessive force against detainees during anti-corruption protests last year in Belgrade, the country’s interior ministry ⁠said.

Anti-corruption protests swept ⁠across Serbia, ​a candidate for European Union membership, in 2025 and 2026 after 16 people died when a concrete canopy ⁠on a renovated railway station in the city of Novi Sad collapsed on 1 November 2024.

The protests ultimately ⁠resulted in the ouster of the populist Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which is ​loyal to former president Aleksandar Vučić, in ‌an 25 October ‌snap parliamentary election by the leaderless Student List.

The ministry said in a ‌statement that the suspects, who served in an elite unit, tortured and intimidated several people detained in the garage of the government compound in downtown Belgrade on 14-15 August 2025.

“By the use of force and threats, (they) inflicted great pain and severe suffering on a larger ‌number of persons, intending to obtain information from them and intimidating and unlawfully punishing them,” the statement said.

The ministry provided ​only the initials of the officers and former officer who were detained. The news marked the first big arrests in connection with violence against the protesters who took to the streets over the past two years.
Police ⁠used teargas, crowd-control vehicles and stun grenades to disperse ​crowds during the ​protests.
Dozens of students and activists ​who took part in the protests accused police of ​excessive use of ‌force that ​resulted in injuries ​and psychological trauma.

Serbian students, activists, opposition politicians and rights watchdogs have accused Vučić and the SNS of political violence, pressure against media, ties to organised crime and rampant corruption. Vučić and his allies deny the accusations.

items.titel: Reaktionen auf Tod Aiwangers: Söder spricht von "absoluter Tragödie"
items.anriss: Der unerwartete Tod von Hubert Aiwanger mit 55 Jahren hat parteiübergreifend Bestürzung ausgelöst. Der Chef der Freien Wähler war leblos in einem Hotel aufgefunden worden. Bayerns Ministerpräsident Söder sprach von einer "absoluten …

absaetze.t: Anteilnahme nach Tod Aiwangers "Eine absolute Tragödie"

Der unerwartete Tod von Hubert Aiwanger mit 55 Jahren hat parteiübergreifend Bestürzung ausgelöst. Der Chef der Freien Wähler war leblos in einem Hotel aufgefunden worden. Bayerns Ministerpräsident Söder sprach von einer "absoluten Tragödie".

"Wir sind alle zutiefst geschockt": Bayerns Ministerpräsident Markus Söder und CSU-Chef hat bestürzt und fassungslos auf den plötzlichen Tod von Hubert Aiwanger reagiert. Er schrieb auf X von einer "absoluten Tragödie".

Aiwanger sei mitten aus dem Leben gerissen worden, schrieb Landtagspräsidentin Ilse Aigner auf X. "Ein großer Verlust für Bayern." Die Fraktionsvorsitzende der Grünen im Landtag, Katharina Schulze, äußerte sich auf X in einer ersten Reaktion ebenfalls betroffen: "Mein tiefes Mitgefühl gilt seiner Familie, seinen Angehörigen und allen, die ihm nahestanden."
"Bayern wird ohne ihn ein anderes sein"

Die Freien Wähler Bayern betonten, Aiwanger habe maßgeblich dazu beigetragen, dass aus einer kommunal verwurzelten politischen Kraft eine feste Größe in der bayerischen Landespolitik geworden sei. "Wir Freie Wähler in Bayern werden seine Überzeugung für eine sachorientierte Politik, die ausschließlich den Menschen dient, mit voller Kraft weiterleben und dafür eng zusammenstehen", sagte der stellvertretende Landesvorsitzende Armin Kroder. Fraktionschef Florian Streibl sagte: "Bayern wird ohne ihn ein anderes sein."
Ein "streitbarer Politiker"
Doch nicht nur in der bayerischen Landespolitik, wo Aiwanger als Parteichef der Freien Wähler, Vize-Ministerpräsident und Wirtschaftsminister gewirkt hat, ist die Bestürzung groß.

Nordrhein-Westfalens Ministerpräsident Hendrik Wüst (CDU) würdigte Aiwanger als "streitbaren Politiker, für den seine bayerische Heimat immer im Mittelpunkt stand". Baden-Württembergs Ministerpräsident Cem Özdemir (Grüne) bezeichnete diesen als "streitbaren Politiker mit Ecken und Kanten, der für seine Überzeugungen kämpfte".
Seit 2018 Koalitionspartner der Söder-CSU

Streitbar war Aiwanger in der Tat. Er war streitlustig, aber auch umstritten. Er war ein Vollblutpolitiker und erlangte - auch mit seinem besonderen niederbayerischen Dialekt - auch bundesweit Bekanntheit.

2008 war Aiwanger mit seinen Freien Wählern erstmals in den bayerischen Landtag eingezogen und wurde deren Fraktionschef. Zehn Jahre später, 2018, schmiedeten CSU und Freie Wähler eine Koalition. Aiwanger wurde Wirtschaftsminister und stellvertretender Ministerpräsident.

Eine Zäsur war der Spätsommer 2023. Wenige Wochen vor der Landtagswahl in Bayern hatte ihn ein antisemitisches Flugblatt aus lang vergangenen Tagen eingeholt, das in seiner Schulzeit bei ihm gefunden worden war. Die Regierungskoalition mit der CSU stand am Rand des Scheiterns, Aiwanger drohte der Rausschmiss - und doch feierte er bei der Wahl wenige Wochen später ein neues Rekordergebnis von 15,8 Prozent für die Freien Wähler.
Staatsanwaltschaft ermittelt

Die Nachricht vom Tod des 55-Jährigen kam völlig überraschend am Mittwochabend. Aiwanger war leblos in einem Berliner Hotelzimmer gefunden worden. Nach Informationen der Nachrichtenagentur dpa hatte er sich nachmittags aus gesundheitlichen Gründen bei einem wichtigen Parteitermin vertreten lassen und war später nicht mehr erreichbar.
Laut Staatsanwaltschaft wurde ein Todesermittlungsverfahren eingeleitet, um "die konkrete Todesursache und den Hergang des Todes herauszufinden sowie ein mögliches Fremdverschulden auszuschließen".
Freie Wähler brauchen neuen Chef

Aiwanger habe die Freien Wähler seit 20 Jahren geprägt und geführt, sagte BR-Korrespondent Achim Wendler in den tagesthemen. "Er war das Gesicht der Partei." Aiwanger habe ganz wesentlich die Wähler mobilisiert. "Für die Partei stellt sich tatsächlich nun die Existenzfrage", so Wendler. Und für die bayerische Staatsregierung stelle sich die Stabilitätsfrage.

Die Freien Wähler, deren politische gewichtigste Stimme und Galionsfigur Aiwanger war, brauchen nun einen neuen Landes- und Bundesvorsitzenden. Als Landeschef war Aiwanger erst vor einem Jahr wiedergewählt worden - als Bundesvorsitzender wollte er sich eigentlich übernächstes Wochenende erneut im Amt bestätigen lassen. "Die Freien Wähler Bayern werden ihre Arbeit im Sinne von Hubert Aiwanger weiterführen", teilte die Partei in der Nacht mit. Ob der Termin für den Bundesparteitag am 14. November nun bestehen bleibt, ist unklar.

items.titel: Marktbericht: DAX nähert sich dem Rekordhoch
items.anriss: Nach den US-Zwischenwahlen ist die Euphorie an den Börsen groß: Der DAX robbt sich immer näher an sein Rekordhoch heran. Hilfreich ist auch der sinkende Ölpreis, der den Inflationsdruck senken könnte.[ mehr ]

absaetze.t: Nach den US-Zwischenwahlen DAX nähert sich dem Rekordhoch

Nach den US-Zwischenwahlen ist die Euphorie an den Börsen groß: Der DAX robbt sich immer näher an sein Rekordhoch heran. Hilfreich ist auch der sinkende Ölpreis, der den Inflationsdruck senken könnte.

Der Broker IG Markets taxiert den deutschen Leitindex vor der Eröffnung des Xetra-Handels ein halbes Prozent höher auf 26.561 Punkte. Damit rückt der Rekordstand bei 26.619 Punkten immer näher. Am Mittwoch war der DAX um 2,2 Prozent auf 26.437 Punkte gestiegen. In der Spitze hatten ihm mit fast 26.542 Zählern nur noch 78 Punkte zur Bestmarke gefehlt.

Die Anleger reagieren euphorisch auf das Ergebnis der US-Zwischenwahlen: Halte die aktuelle Dynamik an, könnte der DAX sein Allzeithoch bereits in den kommenden Tagen testen, meint Salah-Eddine Bouhmidi vom Broker IG.

"Voraussetzung ist, dass die Käufer den Ausbruch über 26.000 Punkte weiter behaupten", so die Expertin. "Die heutige Euphorie verbessert das kurzfristige Marktbild, die geopolitischen Unsicherheiten und das Risiko kräftiger Rückschläge bleiben jedoch bestehen."
"Kein dramatischer Kurswechsel zu erwarten"

Was könnten konkrete Folgen des Wahlergebnisses sein? "Die veränderten politischen Kräfteverhältnisse könnten die amerikanische Haushaltspolitik stärker disziplinieren und damit zumindest einen Teil der Sorgen über die ausufernde Staatsverschuldung und langfristig hohe Anleiherenditen entschärfen", kommentiert Andreas Lipkow, Marktbeobachter von CMC Markets. Die Chancen auf eine Jahresendrally hätten sich für den DAX nun deutlich erhöht.

Das Wahlergebnis sende das Signal, dass die Politik von US-Präsident Donald Trump "nicht grenzenlos durchsetzbar" sei, stellte Dekabank-Experte Joachim Schallmayer fest. Dramatische Kurswechsel seien zwar nicht zu erwarten, doch einzelne Branchen könnten, seiner Einschätzung nach, neue Rahmenbedingungen bekommen.
Ölpreise sinken

Unterstützung kommt auch von den Rohstoffmärkten. Die Ölpreise geben kräftig nach. Viele Investoren rechnen damit, dass eine friedliche Lösung für den Nahen Osten nun wahrscheinlicher geworden ist. Sinken die Ölpreise dauerhaft, würde das den Inflationsdruck senken. Das würde auch die Gewinnaussichten für viele Unternehmen verbessern.
Die Rohöl-Sorte Brent aus der Nordsee verbilligte sich um 1,0 Prozent auf 93,63 Dollar je Barrel (159 Liter). Das US-Öl WTI notierte 1,5 Prozent schwächer bei 86,81 Dollar.
Wall Street legt kräftig zu

Der Wahlsieg der Demokraten hat auch der Wall Street kräftigen Auftrieb gegeben. Der Dow-Jones-Index der Standardwerte schloss zur Wochenmitte drei Prozent fester bei 53.356 Punkten. Der S&P 500 gewann 1,6 Prozent auf 7.688 Zähler. Der Index der Technologiebörse Nasdaq rückte um 1,4 Prozent auf 25.736 Stellen vor.

Besonders gefragt waren die Papiere von Solar- und Ökostromfirmen. Unter Druck gerieten aber Rüstungsaktien wie Northrop Grumman und Lockheed Martin. Anleger rechnen damit, dass das Verteidigungsbudget von Präsident Donald Trump im nun von den Demokraten kontrollierten Kongress auf größere Hürden stoßen dürfte.
Börsen in Asien uneinheitlich

Die sinkenden Ölpreise beflügeln derzeit auch den Gesamtmarkt in Japan. Technologiewerte brachen jedoch wegen der Sorgen um die KI-Branche ein. Der breiter gefasste Topix notierte 1,5 Prozent höher. Der technologielastige Nikkei-Index gab hingegen 0,8 Prozent auf 61.686 Punkte nach.

"Kapital, das zuvor in KI und Halbleiter geflossen ist, wird nun in andere Sektoren umgeschichtet", sagt Wataru Akiyama, Aktienstratege bei Nomura Securities. "Es setzt sich zunehmend die Ansicht durch, dass die Wahlerfolge der Demokraten Projekte für Rechenzentren verzögern werden, wodurch das derzeitige Tempo des Gewinnwachstums möglicherweise nicht zu halten ist."

Vor allem in Südkorea belasten Sorgen vor einem nachlassenden KI-Boom nach den US-Zwischenwahlen die Börse. Der Leitindex Kospi verlor rund vier Prozent auf 5.459 Punkte. Zeitweise war der Handel nach einem Kursrutsch von mehr als fünf Prozent ausgesetzt worden. Die Börse Shanghai blieb dagegen fast unverändert, der Index der wichtigsten Unternehmen in Shanghai und Shenzhen stieg um 0,4 Prozent.

items.titel: Has India’s democracy failed its Muslims? Jailed scholar triggers debate
items.anriss: Sharjeel Imam questioned foundational ideas of India's nationalism in interview with The Quint, inspiring heated debate.

absaetze.t: Has the world’s largest democracy failed the world’s largest minority – its nearly 200 million Muslims? That question is at the heart of a polarising debate currently under way in India.
The debate started with Sharjeel Imam, a 38-year-old Muslim scholar, who gave a lengthy interview to an Indian news website on September 29 from his prison cell in New Delhi.
Imam covered a wide range of issues and raised uncomfortable questions about the place of the country’s Muslim minority, which forms roughly 14 percent of India’s 1.4 billion population.
“There are around 210 million Muslims in India – one of the biggest Muslim groups in the world, with practically zero say in this democracy,” Imam told the Indian news outlet, The Quint.

He criticised the Indian constitution for its “enshrined centralisation” of power and called its brand of secularism “particularly Islamophobic and parochial”, adding that democracy was a tool to deny Muslims their political representation and rights.
Who is Sharjeel Imam?

Hailing from Jahanabad district of Bihar, India’s poorest state, Imam graduated from the prestigious Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Bombay in computer science and worked as a software engineer before returning to academics. As a doctoral student at the Centre for Historical Studies at New Delhi-based Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU), his primary research area was the political history of India’s Muslims.

In 2019, months after winning a second term in office, Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government passed a controversial citizenship law, which granted an expedited pathway to Indian citizenship for non-Muslim refugees from India’s neighbouring countries. The United Nations called the Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA) “fundamentally discriminatory” against Muslims.

The passage of the law ignited nationwide anti-CAA protests. Led by Muslims, mostly women, a weeks-long demonstration near Shaheen Bagh, a densely-populated Muslim ghetto on the southeastern edge of New Delhi, became the epicentre of those protests.
Imam was one of the chief organisers of the Shaheen Bagh sit-in. He was arrested in January 2020 for inciting violence through speeches made at the protests.

But there had been no violence until his arrest. It came the next month in northeast New Delhi where anti-CAA sit-ins organised in Muslim neighbourhoods were attacked by mobs, incited by hate speech from leaders from the governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

Despite him being already behind bars when the violence broke out, Imam was charged with rioting, murder, attempted murder, sedition, and “promoting enmity on grounds of religion” under several laws, including a stringent anti-terror law.

He was not the only one. Nearly a dozen Muslim students and activists, including another JNU scholar Umar Khalid, were arrested and imprisoned for being the alleged conspirators in the 2020 riots. They remain in jail without trial and repeatedly denied bail, with rights groups calling their continued incarceration a “gross abuse of power” and a glaring example of judicial oversight, in which the accused are “guilty until proven innocent”.
According to Imam, such an alleged abuse of power – especially targeting Muslims – is systemic and goes back to the very ideas behind the founding of India as a Hindu-majority country.

In his interview with The Quint, he called India’s independence icon Mahatma Gandhi a “fascist” for making Congress – the party that led India’s freedom struggle and currently in the opposition – an “essentially Hindu party” and for allegedly endorsing certain ideas and practices now pushed by Modi’s BJP and its ideological parent, the far-right Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS).
Founded in 1925 along the lines of the fascist parties in Europe, the RSS aims to turn a constitutionally secular India into an ethnic Hindu state.

Imam also accused independent India’s first Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru of “falsehood and mythmaking” for projecting India as an ancient, “uniquely tolerant” civilisation in his book, The Discovery of India.
But Imam reserved his most scathing attack for India’s pro-secular liberals, arguing that there is no difference between them and the supporters of the BJP and the RSS.

“In short, both secular and Hindutva frameworks share the same core ideas – the myth of uniformity, centralisation and denial of sharing of power,” he said. Hindutva refers to the Hindu supremacist movement championed by the RSS and the BJP in order to turn a constitutionally secular India into an ethnic Hindu state.

In a rebuttal in The Quint, legal scholar Mohd Zeeshan Ahmad said Imam “raises serious historical and ideological questions that cannot be evaded merely because he is facing prosecution,” but that his “equation of secularism with Hindutva is unpersuasive”.
“Imam’s language risks projecting Muslims as a homogeneous political bloc, obscuring disagreements of class, caste, gender, region and ideology,” Ahmad wrote.

“Where are the Pasmanda [less privileged castes] Muslims in this political imagination? Where is the question of gender justice, including the rights of women within Muslim communities? Who gets to speak for the ‘Qaum’ [community], and whose experiences are rendered invisible when a singular political voice claims to represent it?”

But Irfan Ahmad, professor of anthropology and sociology at Ibn Khaldun University in Istanbul, Turkiye, and author of several acclaimed books on the Muslim question in South Asia, told Al Jazeera that Imam is right in questioning whether there is a difference between the Congress and the BJP when it comes to secularism.

“Indian nationalism rests on a false division between ‘secular’ nationalism of the Congress, especially through its figures like Nehru and Gandhi, on the one hand, and ‘communal’ right-wing forces on the other,” he said.

“The fact is that from the beginning, the Congress had within what it depicted as its outside: ethno-racist-Hindu nationalists. The flow of leaders between the Congress and overtly Hindu parties was smooth,” he added, citing Lala Lajpat Rai, K M Munshi, Shyama Prasad Mookerjee, and Madan Mohan Malviya as examples.
“K B Hedgewar, the RSS founder, was himself earlier in the Congress.”

Ahmad, the professor, said the difference between the Congress and the BJP is “of the same nature as the one between Republicans and Democrats in the United States where both converge to advance ‘American interests’ and wage wars outside”.

“The problem Indian Muslims face is not of party politics but the very Indian/Hindu nationalism which all political parties, including the Left, subscribe to, albeit not identically,” he told Al Jazeera.

“If a democracy routinely makes a community, Muslims in this case, invisible in terms of representation in legislatures, then there is something fundamentally wrong with this democracy. Declining ratio of Muslims in parliament testifies to the silencing of Muslims.”
Ahmad says the “question worth asking is: how correct is the view of a secular India?”
On political empowerment of India’s Muslims

In his interview with The Quint, Imam suggested that India should have “constitutional republicanism” that guarantees decentralisation of power and more community rights. He argued that the 1947 partition of the Indian subcontinent – which gave birth to Muslim-majority Pakistan – “was forced by the Congress”.

He regarded Pakistan’s founding leader Muhammad Ali Jinnah as “a great, democratic leader” and poet-philosopher Muhammad Iqbal as his political inspiration. Calling for a faith-based separation of power, Imam underlined Iqbal’s call for the “creation of a Muslim India within India” and demanded proportional representation as opposed to the first-past-the-post (FPTP) system in Indian elections.

“As Iqbal and Jinnah rightly foresaw, FPTP with no safeguards will lead to permanent marginalisation of Muslims who were, even before partition, the hated minority, the hated ‘other’ of the emerging nationalist discourse,” he said. “History has proved them right.”

Responding to Imam, a columnist who goes by the pseudonym Ibn-e-Khaldun Bharati, wrote in The Print news website that Imam represents an “Islamist agenda” which “demands the status of a nation – a Pakistan within the borders of India”.

Calling him “unapologetically anti-liberal, anti-secular, anti-democracy, anti-constitution – in a word, anti-national,” Bharati claims Imam feels “an entitlement to the rulership of India, which has kept their thought-leaders confused about whether they are a nation or a minority”.

“A nation needs a state, whereas a minority needs constitutional guarantees. Neither in theory nor in practice can one be both at the same time,” he wrote. “But such has been the ingenuity of Muslim leaders that they have managed to be both simultaneously. They carved a country for themselves and also secured special privileges as a minority – a classic example of having one’s cake and eating it too.”
Questioning Bharati’s submission, political analyst Asim Ali pointed out “the Kafkaesque nature of the whole affair”.

“This is a man who has now been behind bars for six years ostensibly for a speech advocating a ‘chakka jam’ [road blockade] without any call for violence alongside the even more absurd charge of conspiring to incite the Delhi riots that took place a month after he was already in jail,” Ali wrote in a column for The Telegraph newspaper.

“The space of experience for Muslims like Imam includes not only their personal experiences of discrimination but also of what they have learned about the history of recurrent communal pogroms, the framing of Muslim men in terror cases, the brutalities by policemen and so on,” Ali wrote, citing several examples of police atrocities in the past decades.

While Ali argued that Imam’s depiction of Gandhi and Jinnah is “grossly distorted” and his reading of the pre-independence and partition history as “warped”, he conceded that there is “space for a person like Imam in a radical democratic project that strives for equality and liberty for everyone” in India.

“Imam envisages a role as the head of an intellectual pressure group of middle-class Muslim activists displacing the clerical establishment as the principal voice articulating a ‘positive’ agenda of ‘Muslim demands’,” Ali wrote.
Sharjeel Imam v Umar Khalid: The ‘model’ Muslim

When it comes to the question of future intellectual Muslim leadership, comparisons are often made between Imam and Khalid. Both of them are often accused of being the “masterminds” of the 2020 New Delhi riots and are currently in the same jail in the Indian capital.
But that is where their similarities end.

Khalid, 39, is a left-wing activist who does not reject the Indian constitution – or its version of democracy or secularism – as explicitly as Imam does. He has also frequently cited Gandhi and his message of non-violent resistance in his speeches and writings.

Khalid is hailed by India’s Marxists and liberals as a “model Muslim” who is being punished by an anti-Muslim government for his campaign against the BJP’s hate politics. Global figures and rights groups frequently call for Khalid’s release.

Among them is New York City’s mayor Zohran Mamdani, who, while delivering the inaugural keynote address at the Nelson Mandela Global Leadership Forum in July this year, questioned Khalid’s imprisonment.

“Why must we wait as Umar Khalid enters his sixth year of captivity in Delhi – a political prisoner jailed under the same manufactured charges of terrorism levelled against Madiba,” he said, using the name for Mandela commonly used by South Africans.

It was the second time Mamdani, who has Indian roots, had talked about Khalid since being elected as mayor. In January, he met his parents and left the following handwritten note for him: “Dear Umar, I think of your words on bitterness often, and the importance of not letting it consume one’s self. It was a pleasure to meet your parents. We are all thinking of you.”

items.titel: En Turquie, une COP31 tout électrique
items.anriss: Agir face au dérèglement climatique et s’adapter : chaque semaine, les pistes de la presse étrangère.

absaetze.t: Dans quelques jours, lundi 9 novembre, commence la 31e Conférence des parties (COP) sur le climat. Cette année, la configuration est un peu particulière : deux pays l’organisent. C’est la Turquie qui accueille l’événement sur son territoire, à Antalya, jusqu’au 20 novembre, mais c’est l’Australie qui préside les négociations. “Avec deux pays aux manettes, le risque est réel de voir la situation sombrer dans la confusion et les luttes intestines”, s’inquiète New Scientist.

D’autant que ces deux nations ne se sont pas montrées spécialement ambitieuses en matière de réduction des émissions dues aux combustibles fossiles. Selon un rapport de l’ONG 350.org, l’approvisionnement de la Turquie en charbon australien serait responsable de plus de 75 millions de tonnes d’émissions de CO₂ depuis la signature, en 2015, de l’accord majeur pour le climat qu’était l’accord de Paris. En outre, rapporte le média allemand TAZ, “en tant que premier exploitant de centrales à charbon en Europe, la Turquie a fait part de son intention d’augmenter de près de 30 % les capacités de ses centrales à gaz et à charbon d’ici à 2035”. Quant à l’Australie, deuxième exportateur mondial de ce combustible particulièrement émetteur, elle vient d’approuver la prolongation de l’exploitation d’une mine en Nouvelle-Galles du Sud, le plus gros projet charbonnier de l’histoire de cet État.

Les deux pays organisateurs de la COP31 entendent tout de même se détourner des énergies fossiles et défendent l’électrification comme un moyen de le faire. Le texte qu’a présenté la Turquie en septembre ne s’adresse d’ailleurs pas seulement aux États membres. “La Turquie exhorte aussi les entreprises, les investisseurs, les villes et les organisations à porter à 35 % d’ici à 2035 [contre 23 % aujourd’hui] la part de l’électricité dans la consommation d’énergie mondiale”, détaille Der Spiegel.

Rien n’indique explicitement que cette part d’électricité doive provenir de sources non émettrices de gaz à effet de serre. D’aucuns voient pourtant dans cet objectif une façon astucieuse de faire passer en douceur la pilule de la transition énergétique. “L’idée étant que plus vous avez de voitures électriques, de chauffage électrique, etc., plus la transition vers des énergies propres sera facile”, insiste New Scientist. En d’autres termes, il s’agira de faire passer à l’électricité la quasi-totalité de ce qui fonctionne actuellement au charbon, au pétrole ou au gaz, tout en transformant simultanément le réseau électrique pour qu’il soit alimenté par des sources décarbonées.
Climatiques
Chaque jeudi, les pistes de la presse étrangère pour agir face au dérèglement climatique et s’adapter

La chose n’est pas aisée. Mais c’est peut-être le moment le plus propice pour la réaliser. La guerre en Iran a fait flamber les prix des carburants partout dans le monde et attisé les craintes liées à l’approvisionnement énergétique. “Nous devrons faire des choix, nous devrons faire des compromis, mais en l’état, c’est la première fois depuis des années que trois objectifs sont en passe de coïncider”, fait observer dans Inside Climate News Fatih Birol, le directeur de l’Agence internationale de l’énergie (AIE). Il fait référence au “trilemme énergétique”, un concept issu de la recherche économique et énergétique désignant le besoin de trouver des sources et des systèmes d’énergie à la fois sûrs, abordables et respectueux de l’environnement.

Ce n’est pas parce que ces trois éléments semblent réunis à l’ouverture de cette nouvelle Conférence des parties sur le climat que la transition vers des énergies moins émettrices est pour autant acquise. Mais c’est un tournant crucial : électrification et décarbonation peuvent définitivement aller de pair.
En bref
COP sur la biodiversité : guère mieux que le climat

À la COP17 sur la biodiversité, qui s’est achevée à Erevan le 31 octobre, “les nations ont renouvelé leur engagement en faveur de la protection de la nature, mais restent loin des objectifs ambitieux fixés pour 2030”, résume The New York Times. L’accord de Kunming-Montréal, l’équivalent pour la protection de la nature de l’accord de Paris pour le climat, signé en 2022, est encore loin d’être devenu une réalité. De même qu’à la COP31 sur le climat en Turquie, l’argent est au cœur des discussions. En Arménie, les délégués ont promis “près de 2 milliards de dollars [1,8 milliard d’euros] de financements supplémentaires”, indique le quotidien de New York. Pour en savoir plus, c’est ici.
“Champagne” pour les pétroliers

Le groupe français Total, le britannique Shell et l’espagnol Repsol publient des résultats en très forte hausse au troisième trimestre. “L’industrie pétrolière réalise cette année ses profits les plus importants depuis l’invasion de l’Ukraine par la Russie”, commente le Financial Times. Au Royaume-Uni, Greenpeace a réagi en décriant ces patrons du pétrole qui “sabrent le champagne sur le pont d’une planète qui sombre”. Pour en savoir plus, c’est ici.
Oh ! La belle vague bleue

La vague bleue aux élections américaines de mi-mandat est de bon augure pour le climat, analyse la presse outre-atlantique. Le camp démocrate, qui assiste impuissant au démantèlement des politiques climatiques depuis deux ans, pourrait en effet mettre en place des programmes ambitieux au niveau fédéral. Au niveau local, différents scrutins portaient aussi sur des aspects liés à la promotion de la transition énergétique ou à l’encadrement des lobbys. Pour en savoir plus, c’est ici.
À relire

items.titel: NASA Announces X-70 “Fractal” Experimental Aircraft
items.anriss: NASA just unveiled its latest X-plane, the X-70 Fractal, which Administrator Jared Isaacman had teased last week, at the UP.Summit at Kennedy Space Center today.

absaetze.t: NASA just unveiled its latest X-plane, the X-70 Fractal, which Administrator Jared Isaacman had teased last week, at the UP.Summit at Kennedy Space Center today.

The aircraft is described as crewed and features rapidly reconfigurable flight control capabilities. According to NASA’s release it will “explore aircraft maneuverability in ways never before demonstrated in crewed flight. The aircraft can also accommodate up to 2,000 pounds of experimental payloads in internal and external locations, enabling a wide range of research and flight-testing opportunities.”
The release states:

“The X-70 Fractal gives NASA a crewed, high-performance platform to test advanced flight-control, maneuverability, and other cutting-edge technologies in real flight,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “Its modular design and ability to rapidly swap internal and external payloads will keep our teams flying, learning, and moving quickly from one experiment to the next. We expect her first flight under the NASA banner within the next two years, and X-70 is just one part of this new beginning for aeronautics. This is why people come to NASA: to build, to learn, and most importantly, to fly.”

Additional details about Fractal were provided as having a takeoff weight of 10,000lbs, a ceiling of 45,000 feet and a cruise speed of Mach 0t.75. Its range will be around 1,500 nautical miles. This will allow it to fly across a wide spectrum of conditions and over longer distances and durations.

Described as “generated content,” the image provided is still intriguing. It shows an aircraft with splayed tails, bubble canopy, and fighter-like wings. The concept image is just that, an impression of what it will look like, with much of it cloaked in clouds. It draws superficial similarities to other experimental testbed aircraft as of late, especially those from Scaled Composites, in particular the Beacon testbed aircraft. That aircraft is also a flexible “open architecture”-oriented platform, but it has more to do with testing autonomy packages and drone-related technologies. This new jet has a focus on flight controls and sounds like it will be able to host exotic capabilities in this regard.

Lift fan and thrust vectoring capabilities could also be part of the X-70’s modular potential. There are also concepts such as morphing wings and air-bursted flight controls that would allow planes to maneuver without traditional moving surfaces. These are on the “bleeding edge” of technology and this kind of aircraft could potentially help move them forward.
Isaacman, who flies a private MiG-29 and owned a contractor aggressor squadron, has made pushing aeronautics forward via new X-planes a top priority of the agency’s.

The release also states it will fly “under the NASA banner” in two years. This likely means once the agency takes delivery from the manufacturer or it’s possible this asset is being pulled from the classified realm and ported over to NASA. It is unclear who is building or built Fractal at this time, but we are sure to find out more at NASA’s Max Power air show taking place at the Shuttle Landing Facility at Kennedy this weekend.
This is a developing story, we will update this post in the coming hours as we find out more.
Contact the author: Tyler@twz.com

items.titel: Navy unfairly evaluated Saildrone MUSV proposal, court finds
items.anriss: The court found that the Navy “engaged in disparate treatment” toward Saildrone’s MUSV proposal, according to an opinion unsealed Wednesday.

absaetze.t: PARIS — The US Navy unfairly evaluated maritime drone manufacturer Saildrone’s proposal for the service’s medium unmanned surface vessel (MUSV) program, according to a ruling from the US Court of Federal Claims.
As a result, the Navy must reevaluate Saildrone’s proposal within the next two months, and is barred from spending a large chunk of its MUSV budget until that process is complete.

Saildrone and maritime tech startup Blue Water Autonomy filed lawsuits in June challenging the Navy’s decision to eliminate their respective proposals — Saildrone’s Spectre and Blue Water Autonomy’s Liberty — from the MUSV competition. The companies argued that their platforms met the Navy’s requirements for the MUSV marketplace, which launched in March, and that the service didn’t stick to its own evaluation guidance in the request for proposals (RFP).

“The Court finds that the Navy engaged in disparate treatment, and thus, acted in an arbitrary and capricious manner in its review of Saildrone’s proposal,” Judge Philip Hadji wrote in his opinion, which was originally issued Oct. 30 and publicly released on Wednesday.

The Navy originally disqualified Saildrone from advancing to on-water testing due to discrepancies between the company’s proposal and a summary document known as a J-8 Placemat, which is related to the maximum displacement of the design. The opinion said the Navy “eliminated Saildrone because its Placemat reported loaded displacements exceeded the stated maximum displacement.”

However, the court determined that Saildrone received disparate treatment compared to other firms because the Navy advanced a proposal from Sea Machines despite similar issues involving maximum displacement. It’s unclear which Sea Machines vessel — either the Steamracer of the Steamrunner — the Navy evaluated, the opinion said. However, the court noted that the distinction did not affect its finding.

“Because the Navy accepted from Sea Machines a Placemat that either reported both payload-condition displacements above the stated ‘Max Displacement,’ as Saildrone’s did (STEAMRUNNER), or left those fields blank (STEAMRACER), the Court finds the Navy’s subsequent treatment of the proposals disparately favored Sea Machines and arbitrarily held Saildrone to a higher standard,” the opinion said.

Under the ruling, the court ordered the Navy to reevaluate Saildrone’s proposal within 60 days, applying the same evaluation approach it used for companies that advanced in the competition. The ruling also prohibits the Navy from relying on its previously withdrawn findings under two other evaluation criteria to eliminate Saildrone.
The court also barred the Navy from spending more than $1.5 billion of the $2.1 billion allocated for the program on production until it completes that reevaluation.
A US Navy spokesperson told Breaking Defense that it will comply with the court’s order and reevaluate Saildrone’s proposal to determine if it will qualify for on-water testing.

“The future of naval warfare will be fought on the water, not in a courtroom,” Richard Jenkins, Saildrone’s founder and CEO, said in a statement on Monday. “We are eager to move beyond this litigation and return our entire focus to delivering world-leading maritime autonomy for the US Navy, to help secure America’s future maritime dominance. This ruling is a win for fair competition, for taxpayers, and for national security.”
Blue Water Ruling
However, Hadji reached a different conclusion regarding Blue Water Autonomy, determining that “the Navy reasonably rated Blue Water unacceptable.”

The service eliminated the company from the competition for several reasons, including because it claimed that Blue Water’s test vessel — a twin-hulled catamaran — was not “representative” of its production vessel, an axe-bow monohull.
However, Blue Water Autonomy argued that the Navy deviated from its own evaluation requirements because “[h]ull and machinery plants are not listed as assets to be evaluated in the testing.”

The court disagreed, and the opinion said that “the Court concludes that ‘representative’ unambiguously calls for comparing the test vessel with the production vessel,” and noted that the solicitation did not exclude hull form or propulsion architecture from that comparison.

Even so, Austin Gray, co-founder and chief strategy officer at Blue Water Autonomy, said in a statement to Breaking Defense that “nothing about the test vessel was core to our technology, our ship, or our product.”
Gray also said the Navy has made positive changes in Phase II of its MUSV program the service unveiled in September.

For example, Phase I required proposals to travel 2,500 nautical miles at 25 knots in sea state 4 conditions with a payload capacity of two 40-foot containers. In contrast, Phase II requires that proposals include a payload capacity of at least two standard 20-foot shipping containers and eliminates the high-speed requirement.

“The Navy’s new leadership team has already leaned ahead and fixed problems highlighted by the protest,” Gray said. “The Medium USV Phase II program steers away from the prescriptive, compliance-centric testing rules of the previous competition, a change made by thoughtful Navy acquisition professionals months ago.”

Christopher Miller, Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager for robotic and autonomous systems (DRPM RAS) recently acknowledged some difficulties that Phase I requirements presented for industry. He said the Navy wants to “open the aperture” for new entrants and increase options for other services that may be interested in the capabilities.

“What I’m trying to do is also give more industry opportunities for companies that have something ready to go,” Miller told reporters in September. “Obviously with Phase I, there were some more challenging requirements that they had to meet, and so I’m trying to back off of those so that I can have a healthy, competitive industrial base and really use that to help us identify near-term opportunities to meet our operational demands.”

items.titel: Catherine Meurisse, Émilie Tronche, Blutch… 5 auteurs de BD signent des sérigraphies exceptionnelles pour les 40 ans du musée d’Orsay
items.anriss: Le musée d’Orsay poursuit les festivités de son quarantième anniversaire. Après la collaboration annoncée il y a quelques semaines avec Monoprix , l’institution parisienne dévoile l’invitation qu’elle a lancée à cinq auteurs et …

absaetze.t: Le musée d’Orsay poursuit les festivités de son quarantième anniversaire. Après la collaboration annoncée il y a quelques semaines avec Monoprix, l’institution parisienne dévoile l’invitation qu’elle a lancée à cinq auteurs et illustrateurs français de s’emparer de ses collections comme de son architecture, pour créer avec l’atelier Kiblind des sérigraphies inédites.

Le casting est très excitant : Blutch (Christian Hincker), Catherine Meurisse, Anouk Ricard, Simon Roussin et Émilie Tronche se sont prêtés à l’exercice, et proposeront leurs créations (toutes signées et numérotées !) à la vente à partir du grand week-end d’anniversaire du musée, les 5 et 6 décembre prochain – week-end dont l’agenda sera riche en spectacles, concerts, ateliers, rencontres et conférences, le tout en accès libre.
Des références aux chefs-d’œuvre du musée

Autrice de bandes dessinées imprégnées par l’histoire de l’art (Le Pont des arts, Moderne Olympia…), Catherine Meurisse a travaillé à partir de trois références, l’emblématique Ours blanc (entre 1923 et 1933) de François Pompon, les montagnes brumeuses de Ferdinand Hodler (un « artiste qui m’inspire souvent », confie-t-elle) et la célèbre horloge du musée, pour composer un paysage onirique et vaporeux.

De son côté, l’impayable Anouk Ricard revisite avec de drôles de petits bonshommes équipés de casques de réalité virtuelle La Chambre de Van Gogh à Arles (1889), expliquant qu’elle réalise une vision souvent imaginée : « entrer, tout petit, dans la chambre de Van Gogh, grimper sur sa chaise, toucher la matière des couleurs, sentir l’odeur de la peinture, entendre les bruits de la rue d’autrefois… et pourquoi pas se glisser dans son immense lit pour une petite sieste ».
Des sérigraphies à acquérir lors du week-end anniversaire

Guère intimidé par le format monumental, Blutch s’empare avec un simple crayon de L’Atelier du peintre (1854–1855) de Gustave Courbet, tandis qu’Émilie Tronche, jeune réalisatrice de la série Samuel sur Arte, s’inspire du Ballon (1899) de Félix Vallotton pour « montrer des humains au repos, presque à l’arrêt, afin d’en faire émaner de la douceur ». Enfin, le génial Simon Roussin pose son regard sur le musée d’Orsay depuis la Seine, où il fait flotter l’esprit du Douanier Rousseau dans une composition aussi énigmatique que colorée.
Bon à savoir : les cinq auteurs seront présents le 5 décembre à 10h à la librairie du musée pour rencontrer le public. Leurs créations seront en vente au prix de 450 euros.

items.titel: The midterms are over. Now, as Donald Trump accepts defeat, the blame game begins
items.anriss: Donald Trump famously hates losing and never admits to being wrong. So it was no surprise on Tuesday night when he started casting around for scapegoats after his party’s crushing defeat in the midterms , blaming everyone from lacklustre …

absaetze.t: Affairs
November 5, 2026
4 Min Read
President Trump has been unusually solemn and introspective following the US Democrats’ midterm victory. But with no one outside the White House to blame, where will he point the finger?

Donald Trump famously hates losing and never admits to being wrong. So it was no surprise on Tuesday night when he started casting around for scapegoats after his party’s crushing defeat in the midterms, blaming everyone from lacklustre GOP candidates to Fox News.

No one was expecting introspection from a man who once said that he didn’t apologise because he never made mistakes. But concern is growing in his own circle – and more broadly – that he will move beyond name-calling on Truth Social to a more concerted campaign of vengeance. Since early in his career as a real estate mogul and throughout his political ascent, Trump has operated under the assumption that the best line of defence is attack, attack, attack. And with a Democratic Party majority in both houses of Congress, he can expect two years of relentless attempts to curtail his power and hold him to account. The question is now: who will Trump lunge at first?

Fears that Trump would cast doubt on the results were unfounded. The sheer scale of the win – with the Democrats flipping seven Senate seats and at least 25 seats in the House of Representatives – makes it harder for him to cry foul. Instead he was quick to say that he would accept the outcome. Much of the quaking, therefore, will be taking place inside the White House. Disastrous midterms often prompt a cabinet reshuffle and US media have been reporting an atmosphere of foreboding and infighting within the administration as people try to save their skins. Given that the conflict with Iran and resulting hike in fuel prices have been widely blamed for the severity of the loss, one potential target could be secretary of war Pete Hegseth. Attention might also shift to Trump’s chief of staff, Susie Wiles, though the White House has denied that she could be on the chopping block.

A lot will also depend on the Democrats’ own desire for vengeance. During Trump’s first term, after the Democrats won back control of the House of Representatives in the 2018 midterms, the party launched impeachment proceedings against the president the following year. Those attempts were unsuccessful and it is now understood that the move might have inadvertently bolstered Trump’s long-term support, allowing him to lean into the persecution narrative. The Democrats have therefore been cooler on the idea of impeaching Trump this time around. They could, however, attack other figures close to the president, including Hegseth. Especially since the alleged personal enrichment of Trump’s allies was a key theme in many of the Democratic candidates’ winning campaigns, other congressional investigations could target the president’s friends and family.

Trump appears to be aware that his inner circle will inevitably be in the firing line. “They’ll probably go after me and I’ll go after them,” Trump told Time magazine last month, when he also declined to rule out deploying the military or invoking the Insurrection Act after the midterms. While the latter two options look unlikely, Trump has shown a willingness to use the Justice Department to pursue personal vendettas. He could instruct its lawyers to investigate Democrats who launch congressional probes into his actions as commander in chief. We should not expect much bipartisan spirit, either: Trump has already promised to veto Democratic legislation that lands on his desk.

All-out war on the home front is a possibility but what about overseas? With his domestic powers stymied, the president could go all in on foreign interventions. Ensuring his legacy is one of his chief concerns and he wouldn’t want his bequest to be leaving the US mired in an intractable war in the Middle East. Another possibility is that Trump will become ever more insular, focusing on domestic politics while obsessing over his beloved ballroom and other vanity construction projects.

But the ballroom won’t be built before the end of Trump’s term and the Democrats could use their majority in Congress to investigate or halt the some $600m (€533m) project. Expect it to be another flashpoint in a tumultuous two years ahead in Washington.

Charlotte McDonald-Gibson is a Washington-based journalist and regular Monocle contributor. For further reactions to the US elections, tune in toMonocle Radio. For more opinion, analysis and insight,subscribeto Monocle today.

items.titel: Charles Dickens’ writing chalet and Hastings Castle added to list of English heritage sites at risk
items.anriss: The list features thousands of sites under threat from decay, neglect or inappropriate development

absaetze.t: The cabin where Charles Dickens spent the last day of his life, the home in Stratford-upon-Avon of William Shakespeare’s daughter Susanna and the castle built by William the Conqueror high on the cliffs above the town of Hastings are among 197 buildings and sites added to Historic England’s Heritage at Risk Register today (5 November).

The list identifies sites such as buildings, parks, battlefields and shipwrecks that are threatened by decay, neglect or inappropriate development. There are now 4,991 entries on the register, all of which are labelled as of national importance. This encompasses 197 sites that were added this year.

The miniature Swiss chalet which became the writing retreat of Charles Dickens was a Christmas gift to the author in 1864, arrived flat packed in 94 pieces, and was put together by a theatre carpenter after Dickens and his house guests failed. Dickens placed it at the furthest end of the garden, reached by a tunnel he built under the road at his last home, Gad’s Hill, near Rochester in Kent. He spent much of 9 June 1870 working in the chalet on The Mystery of Edwin Drood, before returning to the house where he died that night, aged just 58.The house, now a school, and tunnel survive, but the chalet was moved in the 1960s to the garden of Eastgate House in Rochester, where it is now too fragile for public access.

Hall’s Croft, an imposing timber-framed building dating from 1613, was the home of Susanna Shakespeare and her husband John Hall.After many uses, and residents including the playwright George Bernard Shaw and the bestselling Victorian romantic novelist Marie Corelli, it was acquired by the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust and opened to the public in 1951.It had already been closed for several years for extensive conservation work when, in October 2025, a car reversed into the facade and caused further serious damage.The playwright Ken Ludwig has donated £1m to the work but major fundraising will still be needed.

Hastings Castle was one of the first three such sites built by William the Conqueror after his victory in the famous battle—and is depicted in the Bayeux Tapestry. The site, with a sweeping view across a stretch of the coast, has a long history, with remains of an Iron Age fort having been discovered there. The castle’s commanding site has made it very vulnerable to storms and coastal erosion and there have already been urgent works to stabilise its ruins. Future plans for the site include the creation of a new visitor centre and cafe.

Along with the sites that have been added this year there is good news: 85 sites for which solutions have been found, and which have now been removedfrom the register. They include the storm-lashed Newlyn Harbour in Cornwall and a little hut in the Gloucestershire garden of Edward Jenner, in which, in 1796, he performed the first-ever vaccinations.

A pair of elegant Georgian houses in east London, built around 1715 and Grade II* listed, had an unusual saviour: Tottenham Hotspur Football Club, which has converted them—with help from the Lottery Heritage Fund—into artists studios, gallery spaces, and a cafe. The space is run by Sarabande Foundation, which was founded by the late fashion designer Lee Alexander McQueen.

Rescue grants available include the Heritage at Risk Capital Fund and the Places of Worship Renewal Fund, both funded by the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport and administered by Historic England, and the Countryside Stewardship Heritage Service.

The UK’s heritage minister Baroness Twycross said in a statement that the register has a crucial role in identifying historic places in need of support.“Every part of the UK is bursting with history, so it is vital we protect the heritage sites at the heart of communities which help tell the stories of our nation.”

Claudia Kenyatta and Emma Squire, the joint chief executives of Historic England, said the most effective way of protecting the sites was to bring them back into use.“The sites saved and removed from the Register this year show what can be achieved when partners and communities work together to deliver positive lasting change.”

absaetze.t: The 56-year-old man is accountable for a "cold, calculated murder-for-hire plot," said US Attorney Jamie McDonald.
November 4, 2026 — 2 min read

Daniel Sikkema, 56, has been sentenced to life in prison for his role in the murder-for-hire of his estranged husband, New York art dealer Brent Sikkema, the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) announced today, November 4.

Brent Sikkema, the 75-year-old co-owner of the Manhattan gallery Sikkema Jenkins & Company, was found dead in his Rio de Janeiro residence in January 2024. He was stabbed 18 times. Two months after the incident, Daniel Sikkema was arrested in Manhattan on charges of passport fraud and later received additional counts of murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder for hire, and conspiracy to murder a person in a foreign country. A federal jury found him guilty on those charges following a two-week trial in May.

"Today’s life sentence holds Daniel Sikkema accountable for a cold, calculated murder-for-hire plot that resulted in the murder of his husband, Brent Sikkema,” US Attorney Jamie McDonald said in a press release. Daniel Sikkema was also sentenced to five years of supervised release.

“For months, the defendant manipulated friends, family, and employees to execute a killing driven by greed. His actions demonstrated a profound disregard for human life and the rule of law," McDonald continued.

Daniel Sikkema had paid the couple's former security guard, Alejandro Prevez, to kill his husband as their divorce proceedings dragged on. Shortly after the fatal stabbing, Daniel Sikkema sent $5,000 to Prevez and promised future payments. The former security guard was arrested by Brazilian law enforcement four days after the murder and still awaits charges in Brazilian courts, according to the press release.

Brent Sikkema co-founded Sikkema Malloy Jenkins (then called Sikkema Jenkins Gallery) with his business partner, Michael Jenkins, in the early 1990s, where he showed artists including Kara Walker, Sheila Hicks, and Vik Muniz. The gallery currently represents more than 30 artists.
